h1:
China Hotel FF&E Procurement
Guest Rooms, Lobbies & Resort Fit-Outs
lead: Hotel procurement is not furniture shopping at a larger size. It is a schedule: every item tied to a room type, a handover date and a fire-regulation standard, with a dozen factories feeding one container. We act as your buying office in China for this — reading the BOQ, shortlisting contract-capable factories, arranging samples, and inspecting before anything is loaded.
sub_intro: Most projects touch all six. The value of buying them together is that one consolidation warehouse and one inspection covers the whole schedule.

subcategories.name: Guest Room Casegoods & Seating

mat_intro: Contract specification exists because hotel furniture is used ten times harder than domestic furniture and is regulated more tightly. These are the lines that get written into a BOQ.

materials.name: Contract-grade frames
materials.note: Kiln-dried hardwood or reinforced engineered frames with screwed and glued joints rather than staples. Built for a commercial warranty, not a living room.

materials.name: Commercial upholstery
materials.note: Contract fabrics rated at 40,000 Martindale rubs or more, with foam density specified for the seat, not just the look.

materials.name: Fire-retardant treatment
materials.note: BS 5852 Crib 5 or CAL 117 depending on your market, applied to foam, fabric and filling. Ask for the certificate by item, not by supplier.

materials.name: Casegoods surfaces
materials.note: High-pressure laminate, veneer or lacquer on engineered board, specified for wear, cleanability and replacement cycles.

materials.name: Metal & stone
materials.note: Powder-coated steel and aluminium, stainless, marble and sintered stone for reception desks and high-traffic public areas.

materials.name: Bedding & towelling
materials.note: Thread count, GSM and fibre content specified per item, with commercial laundering durability in mind rather than retail softness.

buy_intro: Project procurement runs on a schedule rather than a product link. These are the ranges that shape the plan.

buying.label: Typical MOQ
buying.note: Procured against room count. Custom contract pieces generally begin at ten to thirty rooms per item, with stocked items available in smaller numbers.

buying.label: Lead time
buying.note: Sixty to one hundred and twenty days from approved drawings to container loading, depending on how much is bespoke and how many factories are involved.

buying.label: Sampling
buying.note: A mock-up room or a set of material samples is standard before bulk production. It is the single cheapest way to avoid a container of the wrong thing.

buying.label: Packaging
buying.note: Room-packed and labelled by room type and floor, so installation crews unpack in sequence instead of sorting on site.

buying.label: Compliance
buying.note: BS 5852 Crib 5 or CAL 117 fire retardancy, EN standards for contract seating, and electrical certification on all installed lighting.

buy_footnote: On a project, the schedule is the deliverable. We quote dates alongside prices, and we flag slippage as soon as a factory shows it.
check_intro: A BOQ is enough to start. These six answers turn it into a schedule we can hold a factory to.
checklist: Room types and counts, with the item list per room type
Handover date, and whether installation is phased by floor or by wing
Fire-retardancy standard for your market, stated per item category
Which items are bespoke to a drawing and which can be bought from stock
Whether a mock-up room or material sample approval is required before bulk
Consolidation and shipping plan: one container, part load, or staged deliveries
check_footnote: Send the BOQ even if it is unfinished. We will tell you which lines are straightforward and which will drive the schedule.

compare.h2_em: when one party owns the schedule.
compare.intro: A fit-out involves more factories than any buyer wants to manage individually. The risk is not price, it is timing and mismatch.
diy: A dozen factories on a dozen schedules, each with its own slippage
Fire certificates collected item by item, often late
Colour and finish matched across factories by photograph
Separate shipments, so a room cannot be installed until all arrive
Balance paid before anything has been inspected
oz: One schedule owned by one party, with slippage flagged early
Fire and compliance documents collected per item before loading
A sealed approved sample or mock-up room as the reference standard
Everything consolidated, room-packed and labelled for installation
Pre-shipment AQL inspection with photos before the balance is released

faq_intro: These are the questions project buyers ask before handing over drawings.

faq.q: Can you pack and label by room?
faq.a: Yes, and on a fit-out it is worth insisting on. We pack by room type and label by room and floor, so the installation crew unpacks in sequence instead of sorting a container on site. It costs a little more in the warehouse and saves considerably more in labour and delay at the other end.

faq.q: How long does a hotel fit-out take to procure?
faq.a: Sixty to one hundred and twenty days from approved drawings to container loading is typical, depending on how much is bespoke. Custom casegoods and upholstery drive the schedule; stocked items are much faster. We give you dated milestones at the start and flag any factory slippage as soon as it appears, not at the end.

faq.q: Can you build a mock-up room first?
faq.a: Yes, and we recommend it for anything bespoke. A mock-up room, or a full set of material and finish samples if a room is impractical, settles comfort, colour and build quality before a container is committed. It is the cheapest insurance available on a project of this size.

faq.q: Will you work from our designer's drawings and BOQ?
faq.a: Yes. We work from the designer's drawings, BOQ, FF&E schedule or reference images, and we will tell you where a specified item is difficult to source or better quoted elsewhere. We are also used to working under NDA, and will sign before any drawing is opened.
